name: Outbound LinkedIn DM Rubric (Diagnostic Style)
description: Score an outbound LinkedIn DM using specific, testable criteria. Designed like a diagnostic rubric - checks for presence/absence of specific elements rather than subjective quality. Max ~45 points before penalties. Target distribution: most messages 8-18.

sections.title: Fit Analysis Accuracy
criteria: +6: Identifies the SPECIFIC skill/experience from profile that maps to a SPECIFIC role requirement (not generic 'your experience fits')
+5: Explains HOW a listed accomplishment transfers to the role (mechanism, not just assertion)
+4: Acknowledges at least one gap, concern, or reason candidate might hesitate
+4: For edge cases only: explicitly addresses the mismatch (wrong domain, seniority, location, etc.)
+3: Distinguishes between directly relevant vs. transferable experience
+3: References something from the job description that connects to candidate's background
+2: Notes candidate's job search status or likely motivation based on profile signals
penalties: -8: Ignores fundamental qualification mismatch (e.g., no PhD when required, wrong domain entirely)
-6: States fit without ANY explanation of why/how (e.g., 'your background is perfect')
-6: Ignores obvious red flags: job hopping (3+ roles in 3 years), employment gaps, outdated experience (5+ years stale)
-5: Treats sparse/vague profile as if it contained detailed accomplishments
-4: Misreads profile (e.g., says 'your ML experience' when profile shows no ML)
-4: Ignores location/timezone/visa mismatch for onsite role

sections.title: Personalization Specificity
criteria: +5: Names a specific project, paper, company, or metric from profile (not just skills list)
+5: Explains WHY that specific detail matters for THIS role (not just that it exists)
+4: Makes a non-obvious connection (something that required inference, not keyword matching)
+3: References candidate's specialization or sub-domain accurately
+2: Acknowledges career trajectory or progression pattern
+2: Uses information that wouldn't appear in a generic search (deep profile read)
penalties: -8: Uses filler phrases: 'your impressive background', 'your extensive experience', 'your expertise in X'
-6: Only personalization is candidate's name
-5: Lists profile keywords without connecting them to role
-5: Copy-pastes or paraphrases profile text verbatim
-4: Personalization could apply to anyone in same field (e.g., 'as a data scientist, you know...')
-3: Gets a detail wrong (wrong company name, wrong specialization, wrong credential)

sections.title: Role-Specific Value Proposition
criteria: +4: States something specific about THIS role (not generic company pitch)
+3: Connects role specifics to candidate's likely interests based on profile
+3: Addresses a likely objection or concern candidate would have
+2: Mentions concrete opportunity: specific challenge, project, growth path, or impact
penalties: -5: Uses generic startup buzzwords: 'fast-paced', 'innovative', 'cutting-edge', 'mission-driven', 'disrupting'
-4: Value prop could describe any company/role (interchangeable)
-3: No attempt to explain why candidate should care
-3: Oversells with hyperbole: 'incredible opportunity', 'amazing team', 'revolutionizing'

sections.title: Communication Quality
criteria: +3: Has clear, specific, low-friction CTA (e.g., '15-min call' not 'send your resume')
+2: Appropriate length: 60-130 words
+2: Sounds like a human wrote it for this person (not template)
+1: Appropriate tone for LinkedIn (professional but not stiff)
penalties: -5: Obviously templated (fill-in-the-blank structure, recognizable patterns)
-4: Excessive flattery: 'I was blown away', 'incredibly impressed', 'outstanding'
-3: No CTA or unclear next step
-3: Over 150 words (wall of text)
-2: Under 40 words (too thin)
-2: Desperate/pushy tone or multiple asks

global_penalties: -12: Hallucinated facts about candidate (wrong company, fake project, wrong name, invented credential)
-10: Hallucinated facts about role (wrong title, made-up requirements, wrong company details)
-8: Message could be sent to almost anyone with <5 word changes (template test)
-6: Complete failure to acknowledge why reaching out despite clear mismatch
-5: Claims to be 'impressed' or 'excited' by sparse/vague profile with no real content

perfect_fit_candidate.description: PhD Economist, 15 years at Fed, published, for Economics Tutor role
perfect_fit_candidate.weak_response_example: Your economics background and PhD make you a great fit for our tutor role!
perfect_fit_candidate.weak_response_score: 6-10 (generic fit statement, no specific connection, no acknowledgment of what might concern them)
perfect_fit_candidate.strong_response_example: Your Fed testimony work caught my eye - translating monetary policy for Congress requires exactly the kind of explanation skill we need for AI tutoring. The role is quite different from academic research though - happy to share more if you're curious whether it'd be interesting.
perfect_fit_candidate.strong_response_score: 22-28 (specific accomplishment + why it matters + acknowledges they might need convincing)

sparse_profile_candidate.description: Just 'Data Scientist, 5 years, MS Statistics' - minimal info
sparse_profile_candidate.weak_response_example: Your data science experience is impressive! You'd be great for our ML role.
sparse_profile_candidate.weak_response_score: 2-6 (pretends sparse profile is impressive, no acknowledgment of limited info)
sparse_profile_candidate.strong_response_example: Honest caveat: your profile is light on details, so I'm guessing a bit. If your DS work involved production ML systems (vs pure analysis), our ML Engineer role might fit. Open to a quick call to see if there's alignment?
sparse_profile_candidate.strong_response_score: 16-22 (acknowledges limited info, explains what would make it fit, appropriate uncertainty)

red_flag_candidate.description: 5 jobs in 4 years, most recent 8 months
red_flag_candidate.weak_response_example: Your diverse experience shows great adaptability!
red_flag_candidate.weak_response_score: 0-5 (spins red flag as positive, doesn't address it)
red_flag_candidate.strong_response_example: I noticed you've moved around recently - before reaching out, wanted to be upfront that we're looking for someone to own a 2+ year roadmap. If the moves were circumstantial vs preference, would love to hear what you're looking for next.
red_flag_candidate.strong_response_score: 18-24 (addresses red flag directly, gives candidate chance to explain)

domain_mismatch_candidate.description: Computer vision PhD for LLM role
domain_mismatch_candidate.weak_response_example: Your ML research would be great for our LLM team!
domain_mismatch_candidate.strong_response_example: Your work is in vision, so this is a cross-domain reach. That said, your distributed training papers suggest optimization intuition that transfers. If you're open to pivoting, happy to discuss what ramping into LLMs looks like here.
domain_mismatch_candidate.strong_response_score: 20-26 (acknowledges mismatch, identifies specific transferable skill, explains rationale)

scoring_guidance.30-45: Exceptional. Hits most positive criteria, avoids penalties, demonstrates genuine insight. VERY RARE.
scoring_guidance.20-29: Strong. Multiple specific connections, acknowledges complexity, few penalties. Should be uncommon.
scoring_guidance.12-19: Adequate. Some specific personalization but misses connections or triggers minor penalties. Most decent attempts.
scoring_guidance.6-11: Weak. Generic language, surface matching, or ignores fit issues.
scoring_guidance.0-5: Poor. Template-like, hallucinations, or major red flag oversights.

grader_instructions: Score by COUNTING specific criteria met and penalties triggered. Be literal - if the message doesn't explicitly acknowledge a mismatch, don't give credit for 'implying' it. If you see template phrases from the penalty list, apply the penalty. Most messages from capable models should score 10-18. Scores above 25 require genuinely insightful connections.
